lessons.title: Introduction to SQL
lessons.description: Discover the language that powers databases worldwide

theorySlides.title: What is SQL? 🗄️
theorySlides.content:
SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for working with databases. It's used by millions of applications worldwide to store, retrieve, and manage data.

SQL allows you to:
• Store data in organized tables
• Retrieve exactly the data you need
• Update and delete information
• Create complex reports and analysis

theorySlides.title: Understanding Databases
theorySlides.content:
A database is like a digital filing cabinet. It contains tables, which are like spreadsheets with rows and columns.

📊 Table Example: "users"
┌────┬──────────┬─────────────────┐
│ id │ name     │ email           │
├────┼──────────┼─────────────────┤
│ 1  │ Alice    │ alice@email.com │
│ 2  │ Bob      │ bob@email.com   │
└────┴──────────┴─────────────────┘

Each row is a record, each column is a field.

theorySlides.title: Your First SELECT Query
theorySlides.content: The SELECT statement retrieves data from a database. It's the most common SQL command you'll use.

questions.question: What does SQL stand for?
questions.explanation: SQL stands for Structured Query Language. It's the standard language for managing and querying relational databases.

questions.question: What does the * symbol mean in SELECT * FROM users?
questions.explanation: The asterisk (*) is a wildcard that means "all columns". SELECT * retrieves every column from the specified table.

questions.question: In a database table, what is a row called?
questions.explanation: Each row in a table is called a record. It represents a single entry with values for each column.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to specify which table to query?
questions.explanation: The FROM keyword specifies which table to retrieve data from. Example: SELECT name FROM users.

questions.question: What is the purpose of SQL?
questions.explanation: SQL is specifically designed to manage and query relational databases, allowing you to store, retrieve, update, and delete data.

codingChallenge.title: Your First Query
codingChallenge.description: Write a SQL query to select ALL columns from the "products" table.
codingChallenge.starterCode: -- Select all columns from the products table
codingChallenge.hint: Use SELECT * to get all columns, and FROM to specify the table name.

lessons.title: SELECT Basics
lessons.description: Master the fundamentals of querying data

theorySlides.title: Selecting Specific Columns 📋
theorySlides.content: Instead of selecting everything with *, you can choose exactly which columns you need. This is more efficient and makes your queries clearer.

theorySlides.title: Filtering with WHERE
theorySlides.content: The WHERE clause filters results to show only rows that match a condition. It's like asking "show me only the items that..."

theorySlides.title: Comparison Operators
theorySlides.content:
SQL supports various operators for comparing values:

• = Equal to
• != or <> Not equal to
• > Greater than
• < Less than
• >= Greater than or equal
• <= Less than or equal

questions.question: How do you select only the "name" and "email" columns from a "users" table?
questions.explanation: List the column names separated by commas after SELECT: SELECT name, email FROM users;

questions.question: Which keyword is used to filter results?
questions.explanation: The WHERE clause is used to filter records that match a specific condition.

questions.question: How do you find products where price is greater than 100?
questions.explanation: Use WHERE with the > operator: WHERE price > 100

questions.question: What operator means "not equal to" in SQL?
questions.explanation: In SQL, both != and <> mean "not equal to". Both are valid and widely used.

questions.question: How should text values be written in SQL conditions?
questions.explanation: In SQL, text (string) values should be enclosed in single quotes, like 'Alice' or 'Electronics'.

codingChallenge.title: Filter Products
codingChallenge.description: Write a query to select the name and price of all products where the price is less than or equal to 50.
codingChallenge.starterCode: -- Get name and price for affordable products

testCases.expectedOutput: SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price <= 50;

codingChallenge.hint: Use SELECT to choose columns, FROM for the table, and WHERE with <= for the condition.
codingChallenge.solution: SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price <= 50;

lessons.title: Filtering Data
lessons.description: Learn advanced filtering with AND, OR, and pattern matching

theorySlides.title: Combining Conditions with AND & OR 🔍
theorySlides.content: You can combine multiple conditions using AND (both must be true) or OR (at least one must be true).

theorySlides.title: IN, BETWEEN, and NOT
theorySlides.content:
SQL provides shortcuts for common filtering patterns:

• IN: Match any value in a list
• BETWEEN: Match a range of values
• NOT: Negate a condition

theorySlides.title: Pattern Matching with LIKE
theorySlides.content:
The LIKE operator lets you search for patterns in text using wildcards:

• % matches any sequence of characters
• _ matches exactly one character

questions.question: What does AND require for a row to be selected?
options: At least one condition must be true
No conditions need to be true
Exactly one condition must be true
questions.explanation: AND requires ALL conditions to be true. If any condition is false, the row is not selected.

questions.question: Which is the correct way to match values 10, 20, or 30?
questions.explanation: IN allows you to specify multiple values: WHERE value IN (10, 20, 30). Note that BETWEEN would include all numbers from 10 to 30, not just 10, 20, and 30.

questions.question: What does the % wildcard match in LIKE?
questions.explanation: The % wildcard matches zero or more characters of any type. For example, 'A%' matches 'A', 'Alice', and 'Amazing'.

questions.question: How do you find names that do NOT start with 'J'?
questions.explanation: Use NOT LIKE to negate a pattern match: WHERE name NOT LIKE 'J%'

questions.question: What does BETWEEN 5 AND 10 include?
questions.explanation: BETWEEN is inclusive, meaning it includes both the start and end values. BETWEEN 5 AND 10 includes 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10.

codingChallenge.title: Complex Filter
codingChallenge.description: Write a query to find all users whose name starts with 'J' AND whose email contains 'gmail'.
codingChallenge.starterCode: -- Find users with specific name and email patterns

testCases.expectedOutput: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE 'J%' AND email LIKE '%gmail%';

codingChallenge.hint: Use LIKE with % wildcard for pattern matching. Combine conditions with AND.
codingChallenge.solution: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE 'J%' AND email LIKE '%gmail%';

lessons.title: Sorting & Limiting Results
lessons.description: Control the order and quantity of your results

theorySlides.title: Ordering Results with ORDER BY 📊
theorySlides.content: The ORDER BY clause sorts your results. By default, it sorts in ascending order (A-Z, 0-9).

theorySlides.title: Limiting Results with LIMIT
theorySlides.content: LIMIT restricts how many rows are returned. This is essential for pagination and getting top/bottom results.

theorySlides.title: Handling NULL Values
theorySlides.content: NULL represents missing or unknown data. It requires special handling in SQL.

questions.question: How do you sort results from highest to lowest?
questions.explanation: DESC (descending) sorts from highest to lowest. ASC (ascending) sorts from lowest to highest.

questions.question: What does LIMIT 5 do?
options: Returns rows where a column equals 5
questions.explanation: LIMIT 5 restricts the result set to only the first 5 rows returned by the query.

questions.question: How do you check if a value is NULL?
questions.explanation: NULL requires the IS operator, not =. Use WHERE column IS NULL or WHERE column IS NOT NULL.

questions.question: What does OFFSET 10 do with LIMIT 5?
questions.explanation: OFFSET 10 skips the first 10 rows. Combined with LIMIT 5, you get rows 11-15.

questions.question: How do you get the 3 cheapest products?
options: SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY price ASC LIMIT 3;
SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 3;
SELECT * FROM products LIMIT 3 ORDER BY price;
SELECT TOP 3 * FROM products WHERE price = MIN;
questions.explanation: Sort by price in ascending order (lowest first) and limit to 3 results.

codingChallenge.title: Top Products
codingChallenge.description: Write a query to get the 5 most expensive products. Show only the name and price columns, sorted by price from highest to lowest.

testCases.expectedOutput: SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 5;

codingChallenge.hint: Use ORDER BY with DESC for highest first, then LIMIT to restrict results.
codingChallenge.solution: SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 5;

lessons.title: Aggregate Functions
lessons.description: Perform calculations on groups of data

theorySlides.title: What are Aggregate Functions? 📈
theorySlides.content:
Aggregate functions perform calculations on multiple rows and return a single value. They're essential for data analysis and reporting.

• COUNT() - Number of rows
• SUM() - Total of values
• AVG() - Average of values
• MIN() - Smallest value
• MAX() - Largest value

theorySlides.title: COUNT, SUM, and AVG
theorySlides.content: These are the most commonly used aggregate functions:

theorySlides.title: MIN, MAX, and Column Aliases
theorySlides.content: Find extreme values and give your results meaningful names:
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Find the cheapest product price
SELECT MIN(price) AS lowest_price FROM products;

-- Find the most expensive product price  
SELECT MAX(price) AS highest_price FROM products;

-- Combine multiple aggregates
SELECT 
  COUNT(*) AS total_products,
  AVG(price) AS average_price,
  MIN(price) AS min_price,
  MAX(price) AS max_price
FROM products;

questions.question: What does COUNT(*) return?
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts all rows in the result set, including rows with NULL values.

questions.question: What's the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column)?
options: COUNT(*) counts all rows, COUNT(column) only counts non-NULL values
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts all rows, while COUNT(column) only counts rows where that specific column is not NULL.

questions.question: How do you find the average order amount?
questions.explanation: AVG() is the standard SQL function for calculating averages. While option D would work mathematically, AVG() is cleaner and handles NULLs correctly.

questions.question: What does AS do in "SELECT COUNT(*) AS total"?
questions.explanation: AS creates an alias, giving the result column a custom name. "AS total" means the count will appear in a column named "total".

questions.question: Which function finds the highest value?
questions.explanation: MAX() returns the maximum (highest) value in a column. It works with numbers, dates, and text.

codingChallenge.title: Order Statistics
codingChallenge.description: Write a query that shows the total number of orders, the sum of all amounts, and the average amount from the "orders" table. Use aliases: total_orders, total_amount, avg_amount.

testCases.expectedOutput: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_orders, SUM(amount) AS total_amount, AVG(amount) AS avg_amount FROM orders;

codingChallenge.hint: Use COUNT(*), SUM(), and AVG() with AS to create aliases for each result.
codingChallenge.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_orders, SUM(amount) AS total_amount, AVG(amount) AS avg_amount FROM orders;

lessons.title: GROUP BY & HAVING
lessons.description: Group data and filter aggregated results

theorySlides.title: Grouping Data with GROUP BY 📊
theorySlides.content: GROUP BY divides rows into groups based on column values, allowing you to apply aggregate functions to each group separately.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Count products per category
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS product_count
FROM products
GROUP BY category;

-- Total sales per customer
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total_spent
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;

-- Average price by category
SELECT category, AVG(price) AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY category;

theorySlides.title: Filtering Groups with HAVING
theorySlides.content: HAVING filters groups AFTER aggregation. Use it when you want to filter based on aggregate results (WHERE can't do this!).
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Categories with more than 10 products
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS count
FROM products
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;

-- Customers who spent over $1000
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000;

-- WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups
SELECT category, AVG(price) AS avg_price
FROM products
WHERE price > 0        -- Filter rows first
GROUP BY category
HAVING AVG(price) > 50; -- Then filter groups

theorySlides.title: Complete GROUP BY Example
theorySlides.content: Here's a real-world example combining everything:
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Sales report by category and month
SELECT 
  category,
  COUNT(*) AS num_orders,
  SUM(amount) AS total_sales,
  AVG(amount) AS avg_order
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'
GROUP BY category
HAVING SUM(amount) >= 1000
ORDER BY total_sales DESC;

-- Query execution order:
-- 1. FROM (get table)
-- 2. WHERE (filter rows)
-- 3. GROUP BY (create groups)
-- 4. HAVING (filter groups)
-- 5. SELECT (choose columns)
-- 6. ORDER BY (sort results)

questions.question: What does GROUP BY do?
options: Divides rows into groups for aggregation
questions.explanation: GROUP BY divides rows into groups based on one or more columns, so aggregate functions can be applied to each group separately.

questions.question: What's the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
options: WHERE filters before grouping, HAVING filters after
questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before they are grouped. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Use HAVING when filtering on aggregate results like COUNT() or SUM().

questions.question: Which query finds categories with average price over $50?
options: SELECT category FROM products WHERE AVG(price) > 50 GROUP BY category;
SELECT category FROM products GROUP BY category HAVING AVG(price) > 50;
SELECT category FROM products GROUP BY category WHERE AVG(price) > 50;
SELECT category, AVG(price) FROM products HAVING AVG(price) > 50;
questions.explanation: You must use HAVING (not WHERE) to filter on aggregate functions. HAVING comes after GROUP BY.

questions.question: When using GROUP BY, what can appear in SELECT?
options: Only the grouped columns and aggregate functions
questions.explanation: In a GROUP BY query, SELECT can only include columns that are in the GROUP BY clause, or columns wrapped in aggregate functions.

questions.question: What order are SQL clauses executed?
options: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT
questions.explanation: SQL executes in this order: FROM (get data) → WHERE (filter rows) → GROUP BY (group) → HAVING (filter groups) → SELECT (columns) → ORDER BY (sort)

codingChallenge.title: Category Analysis
codingChallenge.description: Write a query to show each category and its product count from the "products" table. Only include categories that have more than 5 products. Order by count descending.
codingChallenge.starterCode: -- Show categories with more than 5 products

testCases.expectedOutput: SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 ORDER BY product_count DESC;

codingChallenge.hint: GROUP BY category, use HAVING to filter groups with COUNT(*) > 5, then ORDER BY.
codingChallenge.solution: SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 ORDER BY product_count DESC;

theorySlides.title: Why Use JOINs? 🔗
theorySlides.content:
Real databases split data across multiple tables to avoid duplication. JOINs let you combine related data from different tables.

Example Tables:
• users: id, name, email
• orders: id, user_id, amount, date

The user_id in orders links to id in users. This relationship lets us see which user made each order.

theorySlides.title: INNER JOIN
theorySlides.content: INNER JOIN returns only rows that have matching values in both tables. It's the most common type of join.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Get orders with customer names
SELECT orders.id, users.name, orders.amount
FROM orders
INNER JOIN users ON orders.user_id = users.id;

-- Using table aliases for cleaner code
SELECT o.id, u.name, o.amount
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id;

-- With additional filtering
SELECT u.name, o.amount, o.order_date
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.amount > 100;

theorySlides.title: Understanding JOIN Syntax
theorySlides.content: The ON clause specifies how tables relate to each other:
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Full syntax breakdown
SELECT 
  products.name AS product_name,
  categories.name AS category_name
FROM products                    -- First table
INNER JOIN categories            -- Second table
ON products.category_id = categories.id;  -- Link

-- Join products with their orders
SELECT p.name, o.quantity, o.order_date
FROM products p
INNER JOIN order_items o ON p.id = o.product_id;

-- You can also just write JOIN (INNER is default)
SELECT * FROM orders
JOIN users ON orders.user_id = users.id;

questions.question: What does an INNER JOIN return?
options: Only rows that have matching values in both tables
All rows from the left table
All rows from the right table
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN returns only the rows where there is a match in both tables based on the join condition.

questions.question: What does the ON clause specify?
questions.explanation: The ON clause defines the relationship between tables by specifying which columns should match (e.g., orders.user_id = users.id).

questions.question: What is a table alias?
options: A way to rename a table permanently
A short name for a table in a query
questions.explanation: A table alias is a temporary short name (like "u" for "users") that makes queries easier to write and read.

questions.question: If orders has 100 rows and users has 50, how many rows could INNER JOIN return maximum?
options: Up to 100 (if all orders have matching users)
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN returns only matching rows. If all 100 orders have valid user_ids that exist in users, you get 100 rows. Unmatched rows are excluded.

questions.question: Is "JOIN" the same as "INNER JOIN"?
options: Yes, JOIN defaults to INNER JOIN
questions.explanation: In SQL, JOIN without a prefix defaults to INNER JOIN. They produce the same results.

codingChallenge.title: Join Orders with Users
codingChallenge.description: Write a query to show each order with the customer's name. Select the order id, user name, and amount. Use table aliases (o for orders, u for users).
codingChallenge.starterCode: -- Join orders with users to see customer names

testCases.expectedOutput: SELECT o.id, u.name, o.amount FROM orders o INNER JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id;

codingChallenge.hint: Use FROM orders o, then INNER JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id
codingChallenge.solution: SELECT o.id, u.name, o.amount FROM orders o INNER JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id;

lessons.title: Advanced JOINs
lessons.description: Master LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, and multiple table joins

theorySlides.title: LEFT JOIN - Keep All Left Rows 👈
theorySlides.content: LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table, plus matching rows from the right table. If there's no match, NULL values fill in for the right table columns.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- All users, even those with no orders
SELECT u.name, o.amount
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id;

-- Result might include:
-- Alice  | 99.99
-- Bob    | 150.00
-- Carol  | NULL    ← Carol has no orders

-- Find users who have never ordered
SELECT u.name, u.email
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

theorySlides.title: RIGHT JOIN & Visual Guide
theorySlides.content:
RIGHT JOIN is the opposite of LEFT - it keeps all rows from the right table.

📊 JOIN Types Visual:

INNER: Only matching rows (A ∩ B)
LEFT:  All from left + matches (A + A∩B)
RIGHT: All from right + matches (B + A∩B)
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- All products, even those never ordered
SELECT p.name, o.quantity
FROM order_items o
RIGHT JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.id;

-- RIGHT JOIN is less common - you can usually
-- rewrite it as LEFT JOIN by swapping tables:
SELECT p.name, o.quantity
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items o ON p.id = o.product_id;

theorySlides.title: Joining Multiple Tables
theorySlides.content: You can chain multiple JOINs to combine data from several related tables:
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Orders with user names and product details
SELECT 
  u.name AS customer,
  p.name AS product,
  oi.quantity,
  o.order_date
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id
INNER JOIN order_items oi ON o.id = oi.order_id
INNER JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2024-01-01';

-- Mix JOIN types as needed
SELECT u.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
GROUP BY u.id, u.name;

questions.question: What does LEFT JOIN return that INNER JOIN doesn't?
options: Unmatched rows from the left table (with NULLs)
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN includes all rows from the left table, even if there's no match in the right table. Unmatched right columns show as NULL.

questions.question: How do you find users who have NO orders?
options: SELECT * FROM users LEFT JOIN orders ON ... WHERE orders.id IS NULL;
SELECT * FROM users INNER JOIN orders ON ... WHERE amount = 0;
SELECT * FROM users WHERE NOT IN orders;
questions.explanation: Use LEFT JOIN and check for NULL in the right table's key column. If orders.id IS NULL, the user has no matching orders.

questions.question: If users has 100 rows and orders has 50, what's the minimum LEFT JOIN result?
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN always returns at least as many rows as the left table. All 100 users will appear, even those without orders.

questions.question: Can you use multiple JOINs in one query?
options: Yes, chain them one after another
questions.explanation: You can chain multiple JOINs to combine data from many tables. Each JOIN adds another table to the result.

questions.question: RIGHT JOIN users ON orders.user_id = users.id is equivalent to:
options: LEFT JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id
INNER JOIN with the tables swapped
LEFT JOIN users ON orders.user_id = users.id
questions.explanation: RIGHT JOIN table_a is equivalent to LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped. Most developers prefer LEFT JOIN for consistency.

codingChallenge.title: Find Inactive Users
codingChallenge.description: Write a query to find all users who have never placed an order. Use LEFT JOIN and check for NULL. Show only the user name and email.

testCases.expectedOutput: SELECT u.name, u.email FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id WHERE o.id IS NULL;

codingChallenge.hint: LEFT JOIN keeps all users. Where there's no matching order, order columns will be NULL.
codingChallenge.solution: SELECT u.name, u.email FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id WHERE o.id IS NULL;

lessons.title: Modifying Data
lessons.description: Learn to insert, update, and delete data safely

theorySlides.title: Inserting Data with INSERT 📝
theorySlides.content: The INSERT statement adds new rows to a table. You can insert single or multiple rows at once.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Insert a single row (specify columns)
INSERT INTO users (name, email)
VALUES ('Alice', 'alice@email.com');

-- Insert with all columns (order matters!)
INSERT INTO products
VALUES (1, 'Laptop', 999.99, 'Electronics');

-- Insert multiple rows at once
INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES
  ('Bob', 'bob@email.com'),
  ('Carol', 'carol@email.com'),
  ('Dave', 'dave@email.com');

theorySlides.title: Updating Data with UPDATE
theorySlides.content: UPDATE modifies existing rows. ALWAYS use WHERE to specify which rows to update!
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Update a specific user's email
UPDATE users
SET email = 'newemail@example.com'
WHERE id = 5;

-- Update multiple columns
UPDATE products
SET price = 899.99, category = 'Sale'
WHERE id = 10;

-- Update based on conditions
UPDATE products
SET price = price * 0.9  -- 10% discount
WHERE category = 'Clearance';

-- ⚠️ DANGEROUS: Updates ALL rows!
UPDATE users SET status = 'active';

theorySlides.title: Deleting Data with DELETE
theorySlides.content: DELETE removes rows from a table. Be very careful - this is permanent!
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Delete a specific row
DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 5;

-- Delete rows matching a condition
DELETE FROM orders
WHERE status = 'cancelled'
AND created_at < '2023-01-01';

-- ⚠️ DANGEROUS: Deletes ALL rows!
DELETE FROM users;

-- Safety tip: Test with SELECT first!
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE status = 'cancelled';  -- Preview
-- Then change SELECT to DELETE

-- Use transactions for safety
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = 100;
-- Check results, then:
COMMIT;  -- Save changes
-- Or: ROLLBACK;  -- Undo changes

questions.question: What's the correct syntax to insert a new user?
questions.explanation: The correct syntax is INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (values);

questions.question: What happens if you run UPDATE users SET status = 'active'; without WHERE?
options: It updates only the first row
It updates ALL rows in the table
questions.explanation: Without a WHERE clause, UPDATE affects ALL rows in the table. This is a common and dangerous mistake!

questions.question: How do you change a product's price from $100 to $90?
options: UPDATE products SET price = 90 WHERE price = 100;
CHANGE products SET price 90 WHERE id = ?;
questions.explanation: Use UPDATE table SET column = value WHERE condition; to modify specific rows.

questions.question: What should you do before running a DELETE?
options: Test with SELECT using the same WHERE clause
questions.explanation: Always preview what will be deleted by running a SELECT with the same WHERE clause first. This prevents accidental data loss.

questions.question: What does ROLLBACK do in a transaction?
options: Undoes all changes since BEGIN TRANSACTION
questions.explanation: ROLLBACK undoes all changes made since the transaction began. COMMIT saves them. Transactions let you test changes safely.

codingChallenge.title: Add a New Product
codingChallenge.description: Write an INSERT statement to add a new product with name "Wireless Mouse", price 29.99, and category "Electronics" to the products table.

testCases.expectedOutput: INSERT INTO products (name, price, category) VALUES ('Wireless Mouse', 29.99, 'Electronics');

codingChallenge.hint: Use INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (values); - remember to quote text values.
codingChallenge.solution: INSERT INTO products (name, price, category) VALUES ('Wireless Mouse', 29.99, 'Electronics');

lessons.title: Creating Tables
lessons.description: Design and create your own database tables

theorySlides.title: CREATE TABLE Basics 🏗️
theorySlides.content: CREATE TABLE defines a new table with columns and their data types. Each column needs a name and type.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Basic table creation
CREATE TABLE users (
  id INT,
  name VARCHAR(100),
  email VARCHAR(255),
  age INT,
  created_at TIMESTAMP
);

-- Common data types:
-- INT: Whole numbers (1, 42, -10)
-- DECIMAL(10,2): Decimal numbers (99.99)
-- VARCHAR(n): Text up to n characters
-- TEXT: Long text (no limit)
-- BOOLEAN: true/false
-- DATE: Dates (2024-01-15)
-- TIMESTAMP: Date + time

theorySlides.title: Primary Keys & Auto Increment
theorySlides.content: A PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies each row. AUTO_INCREMENT generates unique IDs automatically.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Table with primary key and auto-increment
CREATE TABLE products (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  price DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,
  description TEXT,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- PostgreSQL uses SERIAL instead:
CREATE TABLE products (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  price DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL
);

theorySlides.title: Constraints & Foreign Keys
theorySlides.content: Constraints enforce rules on your data to maintain integrity:
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Table with various constraints
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  user_id INT NOT NULL,
  amount DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (amount > 0),
  status VARCHAR(50) DEFAULT 'pending',
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  
  -- Foreign key links to users table
  FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id)
);

-- Constraints explained:
-- NOT NULL: Column cannot be empty
-- UNIQUE: All values must be different
-- CHECK: Values must meet a condition
-- DEFAULT: Value if none provided
-- FOREIGN KEY: Must match a value in another table

questions.question: What does PRIMARY KEY ensure?
options: Each row has a unique identifier
questions.explanation: PRIMARY KEY ensures each row has a unique, non-null identifier. It's essential for identifying and linking records.

questions.question: Which data type is best for storing prices like $99.99?
questions.explanation: DECIMAL(10, 2) stores exact decimal numbers with 2 decimal places - perfect for money. FLOAT can have rounding errors.

questions.question: What does NOT NULL mean?
options: The column can only store NULL
The column must always have a value
The column is a primary key
questions.explanation: NOT NULL means the column cannot be empty - every row must have a value for that column.

questions.question: What does a FOREIGN KEY do?
options: Links to a row in another table
questions.explanation: A FOREIGN KEY creates a relationship between tables by referencing the primary key of another table, ensuring referential integrity.

questions.question: What does DEFAULT 'pending' do?
options: Sets the value to 'pending' if not provided
questions.explanation: DEFAULT specifies a value to use when no value is provided during INSERT. In this case, the status would be 'pending' by default.

codingChallenge.title: Create a Customers Table
codingChallenge.description: Create a "customers" table with: id (integer, primary key, auto increment), name (varchar 100, not null), email (varchar 255, unique), and created_at (timestamp with default current timestamp).
codingChallenge.hint: Define each column with its type and constraints. Use commas between columns.
